new_statements.quote: The basic pattern of Moronene syllables and stress assignment is straightforward. There are two syllable patterns, CV and V, and stress occurs on the penultimate syllable of the word. [...] When any suffix or enclitic is added, the stress normally shifts, staying on the penultimate syllable of the word. This contrasts with many Sulawesi languages in which enclitics are extrametrical, causing no shift of stress. [p.13:] Stress assignment rules: 1. Assign stress to the syllable dominating the penultimate vowel of word. 2. The first vowel of a stressed syllable takes the stress.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the syllable containing the penultimate vowel of the phonological word (suffixes and enclitics included, so stress shifts rightward under affixation/cliticization). Because /aV/, /ei oi ou/ and geminate VV sequences syllabify as a single complex nucleus and the first vowel of a stressed syllable carries the stress, stress can surface phonetically on the antepenultimate vowel (e.g. ['koie] 'that', ['kiiri] 'shave') while remaining penultimate by syllable/rule. Stress is non-contrastive.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Sec. 4.6 pp.14-15: two rules. (1) alternating: in 4-5 syllable words the fourth-from-last syllable takes secondary stress ([,kini'βia]); (2) demarcative: every polysyllabic subunit of the word (prefix cluster, stem, dimoraic reduplicant) takes secondary stress on its penultimate syllable; when the two conflict the demarcative rule wins. Morphemic penultimate stress is overridden when primary stress lands on the morpheme's final syllable (monosyllabic suffixes). A few morphemes (e.g. /sumiarara/, /ʔoŋkona/) carry lexically marked initial secondary stress: 'stress in Moronene is not entirely predictable, at least with regard to secondary stress' (p.15). Monosyllabic prefixes normally unstressed; nominative proclitics always carry secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: p.11 data set (B): with enclitics there is sometimes variation between shifted and unshifted stress ([ʔa'rimo] ~ ['ʔarimo] 'already finished'), shifting being more common; p.12 sets (E)-(G): apparent antepenultimate-vowel stress from diphthongization/geminate vowels; p.15: lexically marked initial secondary stress on a few stems. Andersen 1999:12 also reports Muthalib et al. (1991:25) analysing stress as penultimate except on final long vowels (Andersen reanalyses these as geminate VV, preserving penultimate stress).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word including suffixes and enclitics (enclitics are NOT extrametrical, unlike many Sulawesi languages); data are citation/elicited forms from the Rumbia-Poleang (mainland, Wita Ea) dialect, fieldwork 1991-1999. Family-level corroboration: Mead 1998:16 'Stress is penultimate (non-phonemic), with suffixation usually precipitating stress movement' for all Bungku-Tolaki languages.
new_statements.identity_note: Andersen 1999 explicitly describes the Rumbia-Poleang (mainland) dialect = 'Wita Ea' in Mead 1999/sulang.org terms; the Kabaena/Tokotu'a dialect is covered only by the unobtained Kalsum 1998 MA thesis. Andersen states the mainland subdialects (Rumbia, Poleang) show 'no significant phonological differences'. Glottolog moro1287 is the language-level code covering both dialects. Note a slip in the source at p.14 ('The antepenultimate syllable takes primary stress; the fourth-to-last syllable takes secondary stress') where the transcriptions [,kini'βia] etc. show penultimate primary stress -- the p.10/p.13 statements are the operative ones.
